subject: Geography
title: 8. Political Geography, Tourism and Medical Geography

segments.text: This final unit brings together territory, power, movement, recreation and health. Political geography studies how political power is organized in space; tourism geography studies flows of visitors and destinations; medical geography studies spatial patterns of health, disease and healthcare.
Because the unit is broad, preparation should be divided into three blocks and connected by the common theme of spatial patterns.

items.text: Politics, geography and political geography

: Political geography asks how territory, boundaries, resources, location and spatial organization influence political processes. It differs from political science by giving special attention to space and place.
State, nation and nation-state

: A state is a political-territorial organization with institutions and sovereignty over territory. A nation is a community linked by shared identity and historical/cultural consciousness. A nation-state is an ideal-type situation where political territory and national identity broadly coincide.
World politics and international relations

: Geographic location, access to sea, borders, resources, terrain and transport routes can shape foreign-policy constraints and opportunities, but geography does not mechanically determine political behaviour.
Geopolitics and uneven development

: Geopolitics studies relationships among power, territory and spatial strategy. Uneven development refers to unequal concentration of wealth, infrastructure and opportunity across regions; globalization can connect places while also producing new spatial inequalities.
Tourism demand
: Demand depends on income, leisure time, accessibility, safety perceptions, tastes, marketing, visas and transport costs. Demand is highly sensitive to shocks and seasonality.
Tourism supply

: Supply includes attractions, accommodation, transport, services, infrastructure, labour and destination management. Natural and cultural attractions become tourism resources only when access and services make visitation possible.
Tourism impacts

: Positive effects can include jobs, income, infrastructure and cultural exchange; negative effects may include congestion, seasonal dependence, environmental pressure, displacement or cultural commodification. Impacts vary by place and management.
Global patterns of health and disease
: Disease patterns differ with climate, age structure, income, sanitation, nutrition, mobility, environment and healthcare access. Spatial analysis can reveal clusters and inequalities.
Models in medical geography
: Medical geography uses concepts such as diffusion, accessibility, distance decay, service areas and spatial epidemiology to understand disease spread and healthcare access.
Recent issues and developments

: For current issues, update only from reliable sources. Examples may include climate-related health risks, urban air pollution, emerging diseases, health-service accessibility or overtourism, but the exact evidence should be dated and verified before use.

blocks.text: Political geography: territory, state and nation

items.text: State

: A state is a political organization claiming sovereignty over a defined territory and population. Recognition and effective control matter in international relations, but geography focuses especially on territory, boundaries and spatial organization.
Nation
: A nation is a community of shared political identity, history or imagined belonging. A nation may have its own state, share a state with other nations or be distributed across several states.
Nation-state
: The nation-state is an ideal in which political and national boundaries largely coincide. Most real states contain significant cultural or regional diversity.
Territoriality
: Political actors attach authority and identity to space through borders, capitals, administrative regions, military control, resource claims and symbolic landscapes.
Antecedent boundary
: Drawn before dense settlement or major cultural patterns develop.
Subsequent boundary
: Develops after settlement patterns and may follow cultural or political divisions.
Superimposed boundary
: Imposed by outside power with limited regard for existing social geography. Colonial boundaries provide many historical examples.
Relic boundary
: No longer functions as an official boundary but remains visible in cultural or landscape patterns.
Geopolitics

: Geopolitics examines how location, resources, transport routes and strategic spaces influence power. Classical theories such as Mackinder's Heartland thesis are historically significant but should not be treated as deterministic laws.
Districting
: Electoral boundaries affect representation by grouping populations into constituencies. Malapportionment and gerrymandering demonstrate how spatial design can influence political outcomes.
Federalism

: Federal systems divide authority territorially between national and subnational governments. Geography affects the design because regions differ in population, identity, resources and accessibility.
Capital location

: Capitals can reflect history, strategic defence, centrality, compromise among regions or planned development. Relocation can redistribute administrative activity but does not automatically rebalance the whole economy.
Tourism system
: Tourism links origin regions, transport routes and destination regions. Demand depends on income, time, accessibility, image, safety and attractions.
Types
: Leisure, cultural, religious, ecotourism, adventure, business and medical tourism have different spatial requirements and impacts.
Multiplier effects
: Visitor spending can support employment and local businesses, but leakages occur when income flows to external firms or imported goods.
Environmental and social costs
: Overcrowding, waste, water demand, habitat disturbance and rising land prices can accompany rapid tourism growth. Benefits and costs are unevenly distributed.
Carrying capacity

: Tourism carrying capacity concerns the level of use a destination can sustain without unacceptable environmental, social or experiential decline. It is not one universal number because standards and management practices vary.
Butler life cycle

: The tourism-area life-cycle model describes exploration, involvement, development, consolidation, stagnation and possible decline or rejuvenation. It is a heuristic; destinations do not all follow the same sequence.
Disease ecology
: Disease patterns reflect interactions among pathogens, hosts, vectors, climate, land use and living conditions. Spatial clustering can generate hypotheses but does not by itself prove cause.
Diffusion
: Contagious diffusion spreads through direct or local contact; hierarchical diffusion can move through travel hubs or social networks. Modern mobility often creates mixed patterns.
Access to health care

: Distance, travel time, cost, cultural acceptability and service capacity shape effective access. Two communities the same straight-line distance from a hospital can have very different access because of roads or transport.
GIS

: Geographic information systems can map disease incidence, environmental exposure and service accessibility. Ethical use requires privacy protection and careful interpretation of spatial correlations.
Place and inequality

: Neighbourhood conditions such as pollution, housing, food access, transport and social deprivation can contribute to health differences. Medical geography therefore connects physical environment with social determinants of health.

Use one map-based geopolitical example without turning geography into deterministic slogans.
For tourism, write demand → supply → impacts → sustainability.
For medical geography, link disease pattern with environment, mobility and healthcare access.

rows: Avoid this error Avoid deterministic statements such as “a country must behave in a certain way because of its geography.” Geography creates constraints and opportunities, while politics also depends on institutions, technology and choices.

blocks.text: How to Build an Examination Answer

segments.text: Divide the answer into political geography, tourism and medical geography. Use definitions first, then spatial mechanisms, impacts and contemporary applications.
• Federal Public Service Commission, Revised Scheme and Syllabus for CSS Competitive Examination (CE-2016 and onwards).
• Standard political, tourism and health-geography literature; GIS applications should be interpreted with privacy and ecological-fallacy cautions.
• Territory is central to the state but nation and state are not identical.
• Geography influences politics without determining it completely.
• Tourism creates both benefits and costs that are spatially uneven.
• Medical geography focuses on where health outcomes and services occur and why.
• Connect definitions with mechanisms, examples and limitations; do not present the topic as a list of isolated terms.
